item.question: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
steps_tex: Join $2$ pieces side to side. The joined side hides inside, so $2$ pieces with $3$ sides each give $3 + 3 - 2 = 4$ sides outside, unless two sides line up in a straight line.
Join along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite.
Join along the longest sides, with one piece turned half way round: a rectangle.
Join along the middle sides, with one piece turned half way round: a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Join along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: another one.
That is $4$ different four-sided shapes: a kite, a rectangle and $2$ parallelograms. Sliding a piece along a joined side makes even more, so there are at least $4$.
Check: each of the $4$ shapes has $4$ sides, counted round the outside.

steps_tex: Shape $A$ has $4$ sides. Its $2$ long sides are each the longest side of a piece, and its $2$ short sides are each the shortest side of a piece.
Measure: the $2$ long sides are the same length, and the $2$ short sides are the same length.
Each long side is across from the other long side. So the equal pairs of $A$ are opposite sides, not adjacent sides.
Shape $B$ has $4$ sides: $2$ sides are the shortest side of a piece and $2$ sides are the middle side of a piece.
Measure: the $2$ shorter sides are equal and the $2$ longer sides are equal, and each equal pair is opposite.

A parallelogram with $4$ right angles is a rectangle, so $B$ is a rectangle.

item.question: Now, use 3 triangles from the rhombus to form shapes. How many sides do each one of them have? Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating: (a): a 3-sided shape; (b): a 4-sided shape; (c): a 5-sided shape.
steps_tex: Each piece has $3$ sides, so $3$ pieces have $3 + 3 + 3 = 9$ sides. Joining $3$ pieces takes $2$ joins, and $4$ of the $9$ sides hide inside, so the outside has at most $9 - 4 = 5$ sides. Sides that line up in a straight line make one longer side, so a shape can have fewer.

$(a)$: $3$-sided shape. Join the wider triangle ($2$ pieces joined along their shortest sides) and $1$ more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against one of the $2$ equal sides of the wider triangle. Flip the piece until the outside has $3$ sides. It is a big triangle with $3$ different sides.

$(b)$: $4$-sided shape. Join the triangle with $3$ equal sides ($2$ pieces joined along their middle sides) and $1$ more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against a side of the triangle. The outside has $4$ sides.

$(c)$: $5$-sided shape. Join $2$ pieces along their shortest sides, with one turned half way round, to make a slanted shape. Put the third piece with its longest side against one of the $2$ long sides, and flip it until the outside has $5$ sides.
Check: count the sides round the outside of each shape: $3$, $4$ and $5$. In all, $3$ pieces make $13$ different shapes: $2$ with $3$ sides, $5$ with $4$ sides and $6$ with $5$ sides.

steps_tex: Each new piece joined along a whole side covers $1$ side and adds $2$ new sides, so it adds at most $1$ side.
A piece has $3$ sides, and the other $3$ pieces add at most $3$ more. So $4$ pieces make a shape with at most $3 + 3 = 6$ sides.

$(a)$: no square. A square needs $4$ equal sides and $4$ right angles. The shape with $4$ equal sides that $4$ pieces make is the rhombus, which has no right angle, and the rectangles have $2$ different side lengths.

$(b)$: rectangle, yes. Make a rectangle from $2$ pieces (longest sides together, one piece turned half way round), make a second one the same, and join the $2$ rectangles along sides of the same length.

$(c)$: triangle, yes. Join the triangle with $3$ equal sides ($2$ pieces) and the wider triangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has only $3$ sides. They make a big triangle.
$(d)$: pentagon, yes. Join a kite ($2$ pieces) and a rectangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $5$ sides.
$(e)$: hexagon, yes. Join $2$ kites along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $6$ sides.
$(f)$: no octagon. A shape made of $4$ pieces has at most $6$ sides, and an octagon has $8$.
Check: yes for the rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon, and no for the square and the octagon.

item.question: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Draw two diameters and join their four ends. What is the radius? What shape is formed? What shape is formed when the two diameters cross at a right angle?
steps: The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is half of it: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
Draw one diameter and a second diameter. Both go through the centre, so both are 10 cm long.
Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral.
Check the sides: opposite sides are equal.
Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle.
Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle.
Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle.

3. Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral.
4. Check the sides: opposite sides are equal.
5. Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle.
6. Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle.
7. Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle.
Answer: The radius is 5 cm. Two diameters joined at their ends make a rectangle. If they cross at a right angle it is a square, a special rectangle

item.question: A circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12 round it. Join 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6, 6 to 3, and so on until you reach 1 again. How many lines do you draw?
steps: Find the move: 1 to 5 is on by 4, 5 to 2 is back by 3, 2 to 6 is on by 4.
Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3.
Write the points in order: 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9. From 9 go on by 4: 10, 11, 12, then 1. The thread is back at 1.
Count the lines: each line joins a point to the next one in the list. The list has 18 points with the last 1, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 lines.
Check: 8 pairs of moves (on by 4, back by 3) use 16 lines, and one last move on by 4 closes the design, so 8 × 2 + 1 = 17 lines.
item.text:
Worked example: A circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12 round it. Join 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6, 6 to 3, and so on until you reach 1 again. How many lines do you draw?
1. Find the move: 1 to 5 is on by 4, 5 to 2 is back by 3, 2 to 6 is on by 4.
2. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3.
3. Write the points in order: 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9. From 9 go on by 4: 10, 11, 12, then 1. The thread is back at 1.
4. Count the lines: each line joins a point to the next one in the list. The list has 18 points with the last 1, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 lines.
5. Check: 8 pairs of moves (on by 4, back by 3) use 16 lines, and one last move on by 4 closes the design, so 8 × 2 + 1 = 17 lines.
Answer: 17 lines. The path is 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9, 1
